title: Workflows and agents: who owns the control flow

items.stem: The control flow is whoever decides which step runs next. Who owns it in a workflow, and who owns it in an agent?

options.text: Workflow: the model decides. Agent: your code decides.
Workflow: your code decides. Agent: the model decides.
Both: the model decides, and only an agent uses tools.
Both: your code decides, and only a workflow uses tools.

items.stem: An agent usually costs more per request than a fixed workflow that does the same job. What does it make more of? Answer in two or three words.
Your program runs three steps in a set order: a model call labels the question, the search_manuals tool looks up pages, and a model call writes the reply. Is this a workflow or an agent?

options.text: An agent, because it makes model calls and also runs a tool
An agent, because it takes several steps for a single request
A workflow, because the program chose the sequence ahead of time
A workflow, because it runs a tool and an agent could not do so

items.stem: Which makerspace job most needs an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: Booking a slot after the student has chosen the machine and time
Emailing a reminder to each student 24 hours before a booking
Refusing a booking when the student's training record is missing
Finding out why a student's prints keep failing, with no known cause

items.stem: A fixed workflow makes 2 model calls per request. An agent averages 5 model calls per request. If every call costs $0.002, how many more dollars does the agent cost over 100 requests?
Your assistant must (1) answer a vague question when it is unknown which manuals are needed, then (2) always book and confirm a slot. For cost and reliability, which design fits best?

options.text: An agent for part 1, then a fixed workflow for part 2
A fixed workflow for part 1, then an agent for part 2
A fixed workflow for both parts, so code controls every step
An agent for both parts, so the model controls every step
